The week's most consequential unresolved story is the Oakland Alternative Response Initiative, and it is genuinely unresolved in ways that should matter to this paper through the next several cycles. Rachel Torres reported from the ground level — West Oakland diners, Temescal bakeries, Rockridge lunch counters — and what she gathered was cautious, specific optimism. Server Elio Perez has been hearing neighbors talk about the white-and-teal vans with something that sounds like relief. Baker Melton Neilon used the word "tailored." These are not nothing. A program can generate genuine community goodwill and still be unaccountable. Both things are true simultaneously.

Caldera and Torres are, in some ways, reporting the same program and reaching conclusions that don't cancel each other out so much as describe two different angles of an elephant. The program's expansion comes with unanswered structural questions—most notably how OARI will coordinate with traditional police response when calls escalate beyond their scope, and which agency will handle the program's performance evaluation. What evidence supports the alert — and who's going to step up and tell Fruitvale, West Oakland, and East Oakland what it's actually measuring?

"I've heard people talking about the civic gap, and it feels like the council's inaction is leaving us all hanging — like they're not really hearing what the city needs," Ying said. Two servers, two neighborhoods, same word: inaction. Here's what I can confirm from this cycle. A civic gap surfaced in the city — a live question about who is accountable and what the council has or hasn't done about it.
